title: Getting the Details Just Right: "Pre-questions"?
author: Andrew Watson
summary: Andrew Watson explains "prequestions" -- asking students questions about material before it is taught, specifically questions they are unlikely to know the answer to -- and reports on a new study by Soderstrom and Bjork finding that the technique boosts learning even of content only indirectly related to the questions asked. The study, conducted in real college classrooms, found students answered only about a third of prequestions correctly, yet performed better on final-exam items both directly and indirectly tied to those questions compared to unrelated items. Watson then moves from reporting to offering his own classroom-tested cautions: prequestions likely work because students take them seriously, a mindset that may not transfer to younger students who realize their answers don't count. He recommends using prequestions rarely and only at the start of a unit on its most important concepts, and warns that a prequestion must never accidentally activate a misconception the student wrongly believes is correct. Watson closes by noting that researchers' preferred term, "pretesting," actively discourages teacher adoption because it sounds punitive, and proposes "prequestions" as a more usable rebrand.
points: A new Soderstrom and Bjork classroom study found prequestions improved performance on both directly and indirectly related final-exam questions, even though students got only about a third of the prequestions themselves correct.
Watson recommends using prequestions rarely and only for a unit's most important concepts, since overuse risks students disengaging from questions they know they can't answer.
The single biggest design risk is a prequestion that activates a prior misconception the student wrongly believes is correct -- that actively interferes with learning rather than aiding it.
Watson argues the field's own terminology ("pretesting") works against adoption, since it sounds like a test even though it is really just a set of questions with no stakes attached.
quotes: In this research, students answered prequestions at the beginning of a few lectures. The subsequent lectures then provided answers to those questions.
Sure enough, they did better on both directly and indirectly related questions, compared to the unrelated questions.
Soderstrom and Bjork specifically write that prequestions helped because students took them seriously.
Simply put: use prequestions at the beginning of a unit to highlight the most important concepts.
If a prequestion activates a prior misconception, that question will actively interfere with learning.
But — of course — “pretesting” simply means “asking questions on a topic before you’ve taught the material.” It’s NOT A TEST. It’s just a set of QUESTIONS.
